title: The Day of Uhud
teaser: Fifty archers were told to hold one hill, whatever happened. Forty came down. The battle turned.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: Quraysh came back with three thousand men
layers.content:
Badr had cost Quraysh their leaders and their standing, and they spent the year that followed preparing to take both back. Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl, Safwan bin Umayyah, Abu Sufyan bin Harb and Abdullah bin Abi Rabi'ah pressed hardest for it. Envoys went out to the neighbouring tribes, and men of Kinanah, the people of Tihamah and those living in the settlements around Makkah joined. The profits of the caravan that had slipped past the Muslims the previous year — a thousand camels and fifty thousand dinars — were set aside to equip the army. Poets were hired to talk the tribes into fighting. One of them, Abu Azzah, had been a prisoner at Badr; the Prophet ﷺ had released him without ransom on the single condition that he never take up arms against the Muslims again.

Three thousand men marched north. Seven hundred wore coats of mail. Two hundred were mounted cavalry under Khalid bin al-Walid, with Ikrimah bin Abi Jahl assisting him. There were three thousand camels, and fifteen women brought along so the men would fight harder in front of them. Abu Sufyan held overall command. The standard went to Bani Abdud-Dar, whose ancestral right it was.

Al-Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib watched the preparations from inside Makkah and sent an urgent letter. It reached the Prophet ﷺ in the mosque at Quba', and Ubay bin Ka'b read it aloud to him. He asked Ubay to keep the contents quiet for the moment, went back to Madinah, and called a council of the Helpers and the Emigrants.

The town went onto a war footing. Men stayed armed even during prayer. Sa'd bin Mu'adh, Usayd bin Hudayr and Sa'd bin Ubadah volunteered to stand outside the Prophet's house through the night, and armed patrols watched the roads in.

The Makkan army came up the western route. At al-Abwa', Hind bint Utbah proposed digging up the grave of the Prophet's mother; the commanders refused, afraid of what it would bring on them. On Friday the 6th of Shawwal, 3 AH, they camped at Aynayn, near Mount Uhud.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 8:36 — revealed concerning the wealth they spent to equip the army
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Decision and the Line
layers.subtitle: A thousand marched out, seven hundred arrived
layers.content:
He told the council a dream. Slaughtered cows; a notch at the point of his sword; his hand pushed into strong armour. The cows he read as men of his who would be killed, the notch as a member of his household hurt, the armour as Madinah itself. His counsel followed from it: stay inside the town, let the enemy wear itself out in the open, and fight in the streets if they entered, with the women helping from the rooftops. Abdullah bin Ubai, there as a chief of the Khazraj, backed the plan — not on its merits, but because he had no intention of fighting.

The men who had missed Badr wanted to go out and meet them. Hamzah bin Abdul-Muttalib led that argument: by Allah, who sent the Book down to you, I will not taste food until I fight them with my sword outside Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ weighed both sides and decided on Uhud. When Sa'd bin Mu'adh and Usayd bin Hudayr later rebuked the people for imposing their view, and the men offered to stay after all, he answered: it does not suit a Prophet, once he has put on his armour, to take it off until Allah has decided between him and the enemy.

A thousand marched out; a hundred had armour. On horses the reports conflict — Ibn al-Qayyim mentions fifty, Ibn Hajar calls that an obvious error, Musa bin Uqbah states they had none. A Jewish battalion allied to the Khazraj offered to join; he asked whether they had accepted Islam, and when told no, refused their help.

At Ash-Shawt before dawn, close enough that the armies could see one another, Abdullah bin Ubai withdrew with three hundred men, a third of the force. We do not know why we should kill ourselves, he said. Seven hundred remained.

The camp was set with its back to Mount Uhud, the enemy between the Muslims and their city. Fifty archers under Abdullah bin Jubayr took the one rise giving access to the Muslim rear, with one order. Hold this ground. If you see us snatched to pieces by birds, do not leave until I send for you; and if you see us win, do not leave either.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Jihad — the Prophet's order to the archers at Uhud
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Hill
layers.subtitle: Forty men came down and the day inverted
layers.content:
The fighting opened around the standards. Az-Zubair bin al-Awwam pulled the Makkan standard-bearer off his camel and killed him; the standard passed from one man of Bani Abdud-Dar to the next, and each died holding it. Hamzah cut through their ranks until Wahshi bin Harb — an Abyssinian slave promised his freedom if he killed him — worked close behind rocks and trees and threw his spear. Even so the Makkans broke, their standard left in the dirt with nobody to touch it.

The archers on the hill were watching a victory happen below them, and forty came down for the spoils. Abdullah bin Jubayr warned them. Nine men and Abdullah stayed.

Khalid bin al-Walid saw the ground go empty. He took his cavalry around it, killed Ibn Jubayr and the nine who had held, and struck the Muslim rear. A woman, Umrah bint Alqamah al-Harithiyah, picked the fallen standard out of the dirt and raised it, and the Makkans re-formed around it. Within minutes the Muslims were caught between two fronts.

Then a voice carried across the field: Muhammad has been killed. Men stopped fighting and set down their weapons. Anas bin an-Nadr asked a group of them what they were waiting for. They told him the Messenger was dead. He said: what do you live for after Muhammad — and went forward. Afterwards only his sister could identify his body, and only by a fingertip; it carried more than eighty wounds.

The Prophet ﷺ was at the rear with nine men. He called out — servants of Allah, come to me — knowing his voice would reach the enemy before it reached his own army. It did. Stones broke his lower incisor and split his lip, his forehead was opened, and a sword blow drove two rings of his iron helmet into his cheek. Wiping the blood from his face he said: how can a people thrive who cut the face of their Prophet, while he calls them to worship Allah?

Talha bin Ubaydullah fought over him until his fingers were severed; al-Hakim reports thirty-five or thirty-nine wounds on him, and his hand stayed paralysed.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the wounding of the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud; Sahih al-Bukhari on the paralysed hand of Talha
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: Sixty verses that refused to excuse anyone
layers.content:
Sixty verses of Surah Al-Imran came down about this day. They open on the morning itself: 'And remember when you left your household in the morning to post the believers at their stations for the battle.' (3:121)

They do not soften the account. «حَتَّى إِذَا فَشِلْتُمْ وَتَنازَعْتُمْ فِي الأَمْرِ وَعَصَيْتُمْ» — 'until the moment you lost courage, and disputed about the order, and disobeyed.' (3:152) Three failures, named in sequence, and assigned to the Muslims rather than to Khalid's skill. When they asked how such a thing could reach them, the answer was equally direct: «قُلْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ أَنفُسِكُمْ» — 'Say: it is from yourselves.' (3:165)

The withdrawal before the battle was also addressed. Of the two clans who nearly turned back with Abdullah bin Ubai: 'When two parties among you were about to lose heart, but Allah was their Protector.' (3:122) Of the three hundred who left: 'They were that day nearer to disbelief than to faith, saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts.' (3:167)

Of the men who did not come back: «وَلا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ قُتِلُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللهِ أَمْواتًا بَلْ أَحْياءٌ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ يُرْزَقُونَ» — 'And do not think of those killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision.' (3:169)

Then came the instruction to the Prophet ﷺ regarding the very men whose disobedience had cost him the day: «فَاعْفُ عَنْهُمْ وَاسْتَغْفِرْ لَهُمْ وَشاوِرْهُمْ فِي الأَمْرِ» — 'So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter.' (3:159) Not dismissal. Not exclusion. Consultation.

And the passage closes on what the day was for: 'Allah will not leave the believers in the state in which you are now, until He distinguishes the wicked from the good.' (3:179)
layers.quran_ref: Quran 3:121-179 — the sixty verses revealed concerning Uhud
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: Seventy graves and an order to pardon
layers.content:
The counts. Most narrations give seventy Muslims killed: sixty-five Helpers — forty-one Khazraj, twenty-four Aws — with four Emigrants and one Jew. Of the polytheists twenty-two were killed, though some versions put it at thirty-seven; al-Mubarakpuri records both and leaves it at Allah knows best.

Before they withdrew, some of the Makkans and their women mutilated the dead, cutting off ears and noses and opening bellies. Hind bint Utbah cut open Hamzah's body. Abu Sufyan said afterwards that he had not ordered the mutilation, but that it had not displeased him either. Ibn Mas'ud said he never saw the Prophet ﷺ weep as he wept for Hamzah: he turned him toward the qiblah, stood at his funeral and sobbed. No shroud was long enough — covering his head left his feet bare — so they covered his head and laid idhkhir plant over his feet.

He had the martyrs buried where they fell, unwashed, stripped only of armour, two or three to a grave, sometimes two men sharing one garment. Of each pair he asked which knew more of the Qur'an, and laid that one in first.

From the field Abu Sufyan called out that this was revenge for Badr, that war runs in turns. Umar answered him: they are not the same — our dead are in Paradise, yours are in the Fire. Then Abu Sufyan asked, by Allah, tell me the truth, have we killed Muhammad? Umar said: by Allah, no, and he is listening to you now. Abu Sufyan replied that Umar was more truthful than Ibn Qami'ah, who had claimed it.

That night, wounded and exhausted, Madinah stood guard at its gates. The next morning the Prophet ﷺ took the survivors out again as far as Hamra'ul-Asad, so the Makkan army would see itself followed and not think of turning back.

Carry this. Uhud was not lost to a stronger enemy. It was lost by forty men who left a hill at the exact moment they were winning. And the verse that came afterwards did not remove them from the community — it told the Prophet ﷺ to pardon them, pray for them, and keep asking their opinion.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 3:159 — 'So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the burial of the martyrs of Uhud
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: How many men marched out of Madinah toward Uhud, and how many were left after Abdullah bin Ubai withdrew?

options.text: Three hundred and thirteen, reduced to two hundred
One thousand, reduced to seven hundred
Three thousand, reduced to one thousand
Seven hundred, reduced to fifty

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the rebellion of Abdullah bin Ubai
quiz.scholar_reflection: A third of the army left within sight of the enemy. His stated reason was that his advice had been overruled — but he had joined the march in the first place, which makes that explanation collapse.

quiz.prompt: What order did the fifty archers on the hill receive?

options.text: Fire until the arrows run out, then join the charge
Hold the position no matter what happens — even if you see us being cut to pieces by birds, and even if you see us win
Descend as soon as the enemy line breaks
Guard the camp and the provisions

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Jihad — the Prophet's instruction to the archers at Uhud
quiz.scholar_reflection: The order was written to survive both outcomes. Defeat would not release them and victory would not release them. Victory is what released them.

quiz.prompt: Who killed Hamzah bin Abdul-Muttalib at Uhud, and what was he promised for it?

options.text: Khalid bin al-Walid, promised command of the cavalry
Ibn Qami'ah, promised a hundred camels
Wahshi bin Harb, an Abyssinian slave promised his freedom
Abu Sufyan himself, in single combat

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Wahshi's own account; also Sahih al-Bukhari
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said plainly that Hamzah was his only target and that he killed him to free himself. Wahshi later accepted Islam, and fought at Yarmuk with the same spear.

quiz.prompt: How many were killed on each side at Uhud?

options.text: Seventy Muslims; twenty-two polytheists in most narrations, though some versions say thirty-seven
Fourteen Muslims and seventy polytheists
Three hundred Muslims and three hundred polytheists
The sources give no figures at all

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Number of Dead
quiz.scholar_reflection: Sixty-five of the seventy were Helpers: forty-one Khazraj, twenty-four Aws, plus four Emigrants and one Jew. Madinah, not Makkah, paid for that day.

quiz.prompt: What did Allah instruct the Prophet ﷺ to do about the men whose disobedience had cost the battle?

options.text: Bar them from future expeditions
Pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter (3:159)
Require them to pay compensation to the families of the dead
Say nothing, so the matter would be forgotten

quiz.scholar_reflection: The same passage that says 'it is from yourselves' also says 'consult them.' Being told you caused a disaster and being kept in the room are not contradictory.

quiz.prompt: The archers did not run from danger. They came down because they were winning and the spoils were in sight. Which failure do you find harder to guard against in yourself?

options.text: Losing discipline in defeat, when everything feels pointless
Losing discipline in success, when the rule seems to have served its purpose
Both, but the second is harder because it does not feel like failure
Neither is the real problem — the problem is not deciding in advance

quiz.slider_label: Hardest in defeat — Hardest in victory
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Jihad — 'Despite these strict orders... forty archers deserted their posts'
quiz.scholar_reflection: They were told the order held in both outcomes, which means the Prophet ﷺ already knew which outcome would tempt them.

quiz.prompt: Surrounded and unrecognised, the Prophet ﷺ called out 'servants of Allah, come to me' — knowing the enemy would hear him before his own men did. How do you read that choice?

options.text: He weighed his own survival against the army's and chose the army
A leader who hides while his people are encircled has stopped leading
It was a calculated risk, not recklessness — there was no other way to rally them
It shows what he actually believed about who decides when a man dies

quiz.slider_label: A calculated risk — An act of trust
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the two options before the Prophet ﷺ at the rear of the army
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar sets out the two options in front of him: flee and abandon the army, or expose himself and rally it. He took two seconds to choose the second.

quiz.prompt: 'Say: it is from yourselves.' (3:165) When something collapses on you, how readily can you accept that the cause was internal rather than external?

options.text: Readily — it is the only version of events I can actually act on
With difficulty — my first instinct is to look for who did this to me
Too readily, sometimes; I take on blame that is not mine
It depends whether anyone else is watching me admit it

quiz.slider_label: Look outward first — Look inward first
quiz.citation: Quran 3:165 — 'When a disaster struck you... you said: how is this? Say: it is from yourselves'
quiz.scholar_reflection: Khalid bin al-Walid executed a brilliant manoeuvre that day. The Qur'an does not mention him. It addresses the people who left the hill.

quiz.prompt: The community that disobeyed a direct order was then told to be pardoned, prayed for, and consulted. What does that do to your idea of accountability?

options.text: It separates naming a fault from discarding the person who committed it
It suggests consultation is a duty of leadership, not a reward for good performance
It risks teaching that consequences are negotiable
It only works because the fault had already been named plainly first

quiz.scholar_reflection: The order of the passage matters. The blame is stated without softening, and only then comes the pardon. Neither one cancels the other.

quiz.prompt: The morning after seventy of their number were killed, wounded men marched out again to Hamra'ul-Asad so the enemy would see them following. What do you make of that?

options.text: It was necessary deterrence — appearing broken invites a second attack
Acting before the grief settles can be the only way to keep going
It was almost unreasonable to ask, and they went anyway
It reframed the defeat before anyone else could define it for them

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Hamra'ul-Asad Invasion
quiz.scholar_reflection: He spent the night after Uhud awake, working out that the Makkans might change their minds on the road home. So he made sure they saw the same army behind them.
